title: How Sweden and Austria Compare in English Reading and Speaking
summary: Sweden led Austria by two points in the 2026 EF English Proficiency Index. Austria scored 12 points higher in speaking, and both countries had much larger gaps between their own reading and speaking scores.
edition: EF English Proficiency Index 2026, based on 2025 EF SET tests
sourceReview: On 2026-11-28 the AllRanks assistant checked both overall ranks and all displayed scores against EF’s ranking and country profiles. The point differences use the integer values EF publishes. Appendix A provides the test year, sample, skill-score calculation and rolling index method.

table.caption: Selected scores for the first two countries in the 2026 edition. Values are published whole points. The last column is reading minus speaking.

sections.title: The top two look different when the skill changes
paragraphs: The overall index puts Sweden first and Austria second among 117 countries and regions. Their reading scores are one point apart, with Austria slightly ahead. Austria’s lead is 12 points on speaking. The bigger difference in this comparison is within each country. Sweden’s reading score exceeds its speaking score by 93 points, and Austria’s gap is 82.
Readers interested in spoken English can start with the speaking column. The overall standings capture a wider comparison and cannot tell them which of these two samples scored higher at speaking.

sections.title: The overall index and skill scores use different inputs
paragraphs: EF combines the latest national test average with the previous two published index scores. The reading and speaking figures come from the 2025 tests that covered each skill. EF says about 40% of 2025 test takers chose to assess speaking and writing, so the two skill averages can reflect different groups of people.

EF’s online test was voluntary. Its report describes a sample tilted toward younger adults and people interested in English. The 93- and 82-point gaps compare published averages. Estimating the typical gap for an individual would require matched reading and speaking scores, and extending that estimate to the population would require a representative sample.
